analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from finalizing stricter 2027 tailpipe emissions standards or any rule that limits gas-engine cars.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 221-197 on a nearly party-line vote in December 2023, but the Senate never took it up and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the EPA from finalizing or enforcing its proposed rule setting stricter greenhouse gas and other emissions standards for cars and light trucks starting with model year 2027. It also rewrites the Clean Air Act to prohibit any emissions rule issued since 2021 that 'mandates' a specific technology or reduces the availability of vehicles based on engine type — language aimed at stopping the fleet-wide shift toward electric vehicles. Supporters called it a defense of consumer choice; opponents said it would gut the government's main tool for cutting tailpipe pollution.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers keep gasoline demand from shifting to electricity. Gasoline-vehicle dealers and automakers that rely heavily on gas-engine sales avoid a rule pushing them to sell more electric cars. Buyers who prefer gas-powered vehicles keep the current lineup longer, at least until pollution rules are set some other way.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing its proposed Multi-Pollutant Emissions Standards rule for model year 2027 and later cars and medium-duty vehicles, which would have set stricter greenhouse gas standards starting in 2027.

Amends the Clean Air Act so no emissions rule issued on or after January 1, 2021 can mandate a specific technology or result in limited availability of new vehicles based on engine type, and requires the EPA to revise existing regulations to conform within 24 months.

analysis.who_pays: Households and communities bear the costs of weaker emissions standards: more tailpipe pollution over the life of the cars sold after 2027, continued gasoline purchases instead of cheaper electric operation, and slower progress on climate goals that already-announced auto investments were counting on.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drivers and communities breathing the pollution

drawbacks.text: The bill's premise that the EPA rule 'mandates' electric vehicles is disputed: emissions standards set fleet-wide limits without requiring any particular technology, and its 'no limited availability' language could make it much harder to enforce any meaningful emissions standard under the Clean Air Act.

Blocking the rule leaves the EPA without its main tool for cutting car pollution from model year 2027 onward, so the costs of more gasoline use and dirtier air fall on drivers and communities rather than on manufacturers.
It applies retroactively to rules issued since 2021, disrupting standards already in the works and forcing the EPA to rewrite regulations within two years of enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Buyers of new gas vehicles might see slightly lower upfront prices and more model choice in the near term. But the bill's main effect is to lock out the EPA's 2027 standards entirely, so the public gives up cleaner air and lower fuel costs over the roughly 15-year life of each vehicle sold, while the savings are concentrated with fuel producers and companies that prefer not to retool. The trade runs the wrong way for most people.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 221-197 on December 6, 2023, the Senate referred it to its Environment and Public Works Committee the next day, and no vote ever came — the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Energy and Commerce ordered the bill reported 27-23, and it was reported on September 1, 2023 and placed on the Union Calendar.
On December 6, 2023, a Democratic motion to send the bill back to committee failed 201-214, with all 213 voting Democrats in favor and all 220 voting Republicans opposed.
Final passage passed 221-197: 216 of 220 voting Republicans voted yes and only 5 of 213 voting Democrats did.
The Senate received the bill on December 7, 2023 and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it received no further action for the rest of the Congress.
Because the Senate never voted, the proposed EPA rule the bill targeted was not blocked by this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and gas-vehicle dealers are better off, since the stricter 2027 emissions standards were not blocked. Drivers and communities also come out relatively better, because the EPA kept authority over tailpipe standards and the bill never became law.

for.name: Tim Walberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the House.

for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported out of committee 27-23 on July 27, 2023.

for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage, 216-0 among those voting.

against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, 197-5 among those voting.

against.name: Haley Stevens
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee; the motion failed 201-214.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its December 7, 2023 referral and never brought it to a vote.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote.

against.name: President Biden
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and its blocking of the EPA vehicle rule; the Senate never voted, so no veto was needed.

sides.party_line_note: The final House vote was almost perfectly split by party: 216 of 220 voting Republicans yes versus 197 of 213 voting Democrats no, with only 5 Democrats crossing over.

industries.note: Blocking the 2027 standards keeps more new cars running on gasoline for years, preserving fuel demand that the EPA rule would have steadily shifted to electricity. That gain comes at the cost of more tailpipe pollution for everyone who breathes it.

Dealers and gas-reliant automakers avoid pressure to sell more electric cars, and buyers keep the gas lineup. But automakers that already invested in electric production lose regulatory certainty, and drivers keep paying for gasoline over the life of each car.

industries.industry: Electric vehicle makers and charging networks
industries.note: The rule the bill would have killed was the main federal driver pushing the new-vehicle fleet toward electric power; without it, EV demand grows more slowly. The industry's interest in the rule ran alongside the public interest in cleaner air and lower fuel costs.
